title: DNS records
summary: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT and NS: what each one answers.

steps.title: A phone book with types
body: **DNS** turns names into data. A zone holds **records**, each with a name, a type, a TTL and a value:
- **CNAME**: "this name is an alias, go look up that one instead". A name with a CNAME may have no other records.
- **MX**: where mail for this domain goes; lower preference number = tried first.
- **TXT**: free text, used for domain verification, SPF, DKIM.
- **NS**: which servers are authoritative for the zone.

steps.prompt: Match each record type to the question it answers.
pairs: What is this an alias for?

steps.prompt: You want `www.shop.example` to follow wherever the CDN moves `shop-cdn.cdnhost.example`, without updating IPs yourself. Which record?
options: `A` record with the CDN's current IP
steps.explain: A CNAME delegates the answer: the resolver follows it and gets whatever A/AAAA the CDN publishes today.

steps.title: Reading dig
body: `dig` asks DNS directly and shows the raw answer. `+short` prints just the values.
Useful flags: `@1.1.1.1` asks a specific server, `+trace` walks from the root down, `-x 203.0.113.10` does a reverse lookup (PTR).
On Windows, `nslookup name` and `Resolve-DnsName name` do the same job.

steps.prompt: Complete the command: ask Cloudflare's resolver (1.1.1.1) for the mail servers of `shop.example`, values only.
steps.explain: `@server` chooses who to ask, then the name, the type, and output options.

steps.prompt: Given the zone in the first card, what does `dig www.shop.example A +short` print?
steps.explain: `+short` shows the CNAME it followed, then the A record at the end of the chain.

steps.prompt: Does the record belong on the name `shop.example` alongside its A record?
steps.explain: A CNAME must be the only record at its name. That's why the bare *apex* domain usually can't be a CNAME (it needs NS and SOA); providers offer ALIAS/flattening instead.

steps.title: Look up a record
prompt: A zone is a list of `(Name, Type, Value)` records. Write `List<string> Lookup(List<(string Name, string Type, string Value)> zone, string name, string type)`
returning the values of every record whose name matches **case-insensitively** and whose type matches exactly, in zone order.
starter: List<string> Lookup(List<(string Name, string Type, string Value)> zone, string name, string type)
solution: List<string> Lookup(List<(string Name, string Type, string Value)> zone, string name, string type)
=> zone.Where(r => string.Equals(r.Name, name, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) && r.Type == type)
template: var dojoZ = new List<(string Name, string Type, string Value)> {
Dojo.Eq("two A records", new List<string> { "203.0.113.10", "203.0.113.11" }, Lookup(dojoZ, "shop.example", "A"));
Dojo.Eq("names are case-insensitive", new List<string> { "10 mail.shop.example" }, Lookup(dojoZ, "SHOP.example", "MX"));

steps.title: Pick the mail server
prompt: MX values look like `"10 mail.shop.example"`. Write `string? PrimaryMx(List<string> mxValues)` returning the host with the **lowest**
preference number (first one wins a tie), or `null` for an empty list.
solution: if (pref < bestPref) { bestPref = pref; best = parts[1]; }
template: Dojo.Eq("lowest wins", "a.mx", PrimaryMx(new List<string> { "20 b.mx", "5 a.mx", "30 c.mx" }));
Dojo.Eq("tie keeps first", "x.mx", PrimaryMx(new List<string> { "10 x.mx", "10 y.mx" }));
hints: Split on the space: number, then host.
Only replace the best on a strictly smaller number.
